newsitem.title: JORDAN: Iraq won't seek IMF advice on economic recovery.
newsitem.headline: Iraq won't seek IMF advice on economic recovery.

text.p: Iraq's Central Bank governor Isam Hweish was quoted on Saturday as saying his country's economy would recover from six years of crippling U.N. sanctions without help from the International Monetary Fund.

Hweish, in an interview with the Jordanian newspaper al-Rai, said Iraq shared some IMF policies such as encouraging the private sector, but would not permit the fund to influence its financial policies or prevent it from subsidising commodities.
"A number of experiments, including those by Arab countries, with the International Monetary Fund have not been very successful, either in Egypt, Syria or Jordan," Hweish said.
"We have noticed exaggerated haste in economic reforms, because it is believed that time is not on the side of countries with economic problems," he said.

Hweish said that despite the U.N. sanctions, imposed on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, trade across its long porous borders with Jordan, Turkey and Iran helped maintain a supply of some necessary goods.
"The length of the borders has negative and positive effects. Even if we wanted to control the border areas it would not be possible, so there is widescale border trade," he said.

Hweish said Iraq's financial priorities were stability and an improved exchange rate for the Iraqi dinar, which he said had strengthened from about 2,900 to the U.S. dollar to less than half that amount since agreement on a United Nations oil-for-food deal.
Iraq has said implementation of the deal, which allows it to export $2 billion of oil every six months, is the beginning of the end of the wider trade sanctions.

"What Iraq is going through presently is a severe economic illness, but it is not a chronic illness," Hweish said. "A severely ill patient might die, but he needs less time for recuperation than a chronic patient, like Egypt and India."

"What the International Monetary Fund calls for does not achieve the desired results. We believe that Iraq, relying on its own resources can avoid much of what the International Monetary Fund calls for," he added.
